video_title: The Dramatic Birth of the DVD Boom
transcript: It could have been a disaster. In the mid-1990s,   two opposing camps faced off over  the future of digital video discs. On one side, the creators of the Compact  Disc: Philips and Sony, with a CD for movies. On the other, a disc from Toshiba and Warner  Brothers. Was one better than the other? For some time it looked like  VHS and Betamax all over again.   In today’s video, the dramatic  birth of the DVD boom. ## Loading ... In 1982, Sony and Philips revolutionized  the audio world with the Compact Disc. It was the first mass-market digital consumer  product that the public actually accepted.   It not only offered high  quality audio, it let you pause,   restart, fast-forward, skip  tracks and all the jazz. And the disc itself was also small,  sturdy and came in a nice jewel case. In the 1980s, CD sales made the  music industry so much money.   New, cheaper CD player hardware emerged. Record  labels rushed to re-release their hits on CD.   Retailer chains like Sam Goody and  Tower Records embraced the format. Volumes exploded. In 1983, there were 5.5  million CDs sold. Five years later in 1988,   a staggering 400 million CDs were manufactured  globally. The following year saw 600 million CDs. Moreover, each CD then cost  about $2.35 to manufacture   but sold for a retail price of about $16.  Even counting artist and songwriter royalties,   marketing costs, and retailer margin, there was  still a lot of money left. It was a smorgasbord! ## The CD-ROM Sequel As is the case with any breakout blockbuster  movie, the CD standards body rushed out sequels. The most successful sequel was its immediate  follow-up, the CD Read-Only Memory or CD-ROM.   The idea was simple:   How about we use CDs to store raw computer data  like databases instead of audio sound recordings? Introduced in 1983, it started slow - Microsoft's   First International Conference on CD-ROM  in 1986 attracted just a thousand nerds. The CD-ROM would not really hit its stride in  the 1990s until they finally hit the PC market.   A CD's far higher storage capacity  combined with an audio card,   color monitor, and speakers turned  the desktop into a multimedia device. Microsoft backed it heavily,   putting out a series of popular software products  like Encarta and Microsoft Bookshelf. Later on,   other interactive multimedia like the video game  Myst and the 7th Guest spurred further adoption. The CD-ROM eventually grew into  a massive success. By 1993,   the industry was worth billions and thousands  attended Microsoft's CD-ROM conferences.   Philips felt that more possibilities for the  CD format existed, and sought to explore them. Their next big thing was CD-Interactive. Announced   at that first Microsoft 1986 conference  on the CD-ROM - likely to the surprise of   Microsoft itself - CD-I was a disc storage  plus interactive content hardware platform. I immediately thought of video games - and  I think Philips eventually tried that - but   it was initially positioned for “edutainment”.  Museum tours, family stuff and point of sale.   The company tried hard to promote CD-I  over the next few years to little avail. ## What's to Watch Next? An obvious target was Hollywood and home video. Disc-based home viewing technologies  have been around since the 1970s.   Notable examples include the LaserDisc - a  high resolution format originally developed   by Philips and MCA and championed by Pioneer.  It became a niche success for enthusiasts. But it was instead the cassette-based VHS  format that swept up the market starting in   the late 1970s. Cheap VHS tapes created a brand  new medium for studios to sell their content. VHS also enabled another big money maker: Video  rental stores. Studios sold tapes to these shops   at marked up wholesale prices - like $60  to $100 per tape - which the shop owners   then earned back over time with rentals. (They  would later change this to a revenue share.) By 1988, the US video rental market  had grown to be worth $5.5 billion,   with thousands of rental shops across the country.   All in, home video viewing contributed  over 50% of revenue for the studios. By the late 1980s however, VHS growth in the  form of VCR and rental shops began to plateau.   Meanwhile, cable and satellite competition  continued to loom over the studios. What was next? Companies tried promoting new formats. In 1987,  JVC tried Super-VHS, a backwards-compatible format   with better resolution. The cassettes were  the same as VHS, but the magnetic tapes inside   were of higher quality. Crystal  clear and blemish free, so they say. The Super-VHS format competed with 8-millimeter  tapes. Sony backed something called Video8,   which would later turn into Hi-8. While  8-millimeter tape failed the home video market,   their smaller size helped them become standard in  these ancient history devices known as camcorders. For those who are confused, camcorders are 20th  century single-purpose video recorders. Unlike   cellphones, they didn't make calls or access  the Internet. They just record video onto tapes. Anyway. The VHS seemed unbeatable.  The ecosystem was deeply engrained.   VHS tapes and their players were cheap and  their quality was good enough on CRT TVs.   There were 189 million VCR  households around the world.   Customers used VCRs not just for home theater,  but also taping TV shows for watching later. ## CD Video The CD's first big entrance into video  was with a format called CD Video. Introduced in 1987, CD Video combined CD's digital  sound with an analog video track. Regular CD   players can play the CD-V audio, but you needed  a special player to play the video on TVs.   It launched in several disc sizes, with  the smallest being that of a standard CD. But because the video was stored on the disc  as an analog FM signal and not a digital one,   the smaller disc sizes can only hold about five  or six minutes of video and 20 minutes of audio. The pitch was that audiences can  watch music videos. Same as with CDs,   the first CD-Vs featured classical music and  opera, but the user experience was bizarre.   Five minutes of video and 20  minutes of blank, image-less sound. During the format's development, Philips  demonstrated it to a Warner Brothers   executive named Warren Lieberfarb, who was  then the president of Warner Home Video. Lieberfarb had been growing increasingly  concerned about competition from digital   satellite and cable. More channels means more  people watching cable rather than going to   their local video rental store. He concluded  that the solution was to offer video and audio   quality superior to that of cable but at  an affordable price (about $10 to $12). Spurred by the CD Video demonstration, Lieberfarb  looked at the economics of LaserDisc and noted   that the disc's per-unit manufacturing cost could  be half that of the VHS cassette at high volume.   From then on, he made it his mission  to put movies onto a disc substrate. Lieberfarb pushed Warner Brothers to  establish a partnership with Philips   to develop a new standard with CD quality  sound and video that was at least VHS quality.   Unfortunately, early work centering on the  MPEG-1 compression codec yielded iffy results. A year later, Warner announced  a merger with Time Inc to create   the world's largest media company: Time Warner. Then in 1991, the Japanese companies Toshiba and  C. Itoh bought a 12.5% stake into Time Warner   for a billion dollars. The two were  interested in exploring opportunities   to join their hardware experience  with Warner’s media and cable assets. Warner also needed the money to pay down debt.  When has Warner ever NOT been in heavy debt? With the Philips-Warner work showing  little results, Lieberfarb met with   Toshiba to see what progress those  guys had made on digital compression.   What he saw looked far better, so in 1992  Warner went to Toshiba. Though a year later,   Warners apparently reconciled with  Philips, signing a letter of intent. ## Video CD Philips continued working on the MPEG-1 codec. They first tried to integrate it into the  CD-I platform - striking a 1993 deal with   the Paramount studio for the latter  to provide about 50 movies on CD-I.   Unfortunately this still did not motivate  enough people to buy the hardware. But this work eventually fed into a  new, separate format called Video CD.   No, not the same as CD Video. VCD, not  CD-V. Anyway. Thanks to MPEG-1 compression,   VCD can hold more content than CD-V -  about 74 minutes as opposed to five. Unfortunately, it still competed poorly  against VHS tapes. The player hardware   cost more than that for VCRs and it  cannot record TV. And disappointingly,   the compressed image resolution of about 240p was  only roughly about as good as VHS. So why bother? In the West VCD was panned as unneeded  and expensive. However, the format   caught fire in Chinese-speaking Asia. Thanks  substantially to the efforts of Jiang Wanmeng.   In 1992, Jiang came across MPEG-1 at an  international TV technology exhibition in the US. Jiang partnered with that MPEG company - named  C-Cube - to produce the world's first VCD player   in the city of Hefei, called "Wanyan" (萬燕).  Despite selling for a pricey 5,000 RMB ($867)   per unit, Wanyan sold out its initial run.   VHS had not established itself in Mainland China,  so they were the only show in town for home video. Unfortunately, Wanyan attracted competitors  who copied the device design - which had   not been patented - and spent lavishly  on advertising. The fierce competition   eventually drove the original Wanyan to sell  to the Meiling Refrigerator Company in 1996. But the boom turned VCD into an  established standard in Mainland   China with 10-15 million players sold in 1997. Eventually domestic companies like BBK, Aido and  Shinco emerged with their own VCD players, driving   the foreigners out of the market. VCD lasted  as a dominant format for several more years. Studios did not release much content for VCD  because the format had no anti-copying protection.   But that did not stop people from  filming movies inside theaters   and putting the contents onto VCDs to sell  for cheap - particularly in Hong Kong. ## Sounding the Call Some time in late August or early September 1994,   representatives from seven of the world's  largest content makers gathered together. They called for a single worldwide optical disc  standard that they can use for their movies.   There were a few technical requirements. It would  need to have room for a full length feature film,   so about 135 minutes on one side of the disc. Its picture quality must be superior to that of  an existing high-end video system like LaserDisc.   It had to support surround sound,   multiple languages, and aspect ratios. And it also  had to have copy protection for obvious reasons. The financial stakes were large.   MGM/United Artists' Home Entertainment  President Richard Cohen told the LA Times: > "If a digital video disc solution is presented  in a way that large numbers of consumers look at   it and say 'This is better than tape and better  than LaserDisc', then it becomes a mass product   opportunity for people such as us who control  libraries to sell the films all over again" The record labels made billions from CD.   The studios stood to do just as well or better  from a successful Digital Video Disc format. The patent-holders of such a standard also stood  to reap millions of dollars from licensing fees. Various proposals emerged to meet  this request. Amidst the shuffle,   two large camps emerged with  different but similar offerings. ## MMCD While Warners and Philips  did make some peace in 1993,   Philips eventually left to rejoin Sony  - their successful partner from the CD. In December 1994, they publicly  announced their next big thing:   Multimedia CD, or MMCD. The original  name was HDCD but that was already taken. An MMCD was the same size of an audio CD with  each side able to store far more data - about   3.7 gigabytes. That lets you put about 135  minutes of video onto a single disc side   which met the requirements just barely. The MMCD alliance had signed 14 initial  backers, mostly hardware companies like Nokia,   Bang and Olufsen, and Ricoh. Sony had bought  the major movie studio Columbia in 1989,   so they too were aligned. ## Super Density A month after MMCD's announcement, a coven  of Japanese consumer electronics companies   including Toshiba announced their new, different  standard: "Super Disc" or "Super Density Disc". The Compact Disc surface features a series  of deep pits and flat areas called "lands".   When we read the CD, a laser  scans over the surface.   When the laser light hits a pit, it doesn't  reflect as much as it does when hitting a land. The subsequent pattern of reflections are  sensed by a photodiode receptor in the machine,   which then produces a digital electric signal  that can be interpreted by a processor. If we want to put more data onto the disc, we  need to stuff more pits onto the disc surface.   SD did this with smaller pits packed tighter  together - about 0.4 microns large and 0.74   microns apart compared to MMCD's 0.45  microns large and 0.84 microns apart. This gives the Super Density disc  5 gigabytes of storage on one side   as compared to MMCD's 3.7 gigabytes. SD has a thinner substrate,  about 0.6 millimeters thick.   This makes it possible to bond  two sides together back to back,   creating 8-9 gigabytes of total storage across  both sides. But you will need to flip the disc. Super Disc also offered an optional  second approach for even more capacity:   Dual layers. The first information  layer, let's call it Layer A,   is semi-transparent. The second information  layer, Layer B, is fully reflective. Layer A being semi-transparent means  that it can reflect just enough light   for its pits to be read by the  laser if focused directly on it. But at the same time, the laser can  also fire through it to focus on and   read from Layer B below. I know,  right? Doesn't that sound crazy?   This makes it possible to get up  to 10 gigabytes on a single side. The SD Alliance composed of seven companies,  mostly Japanese consumer electronics companies,   led by Toshiba and Matsushita  or Panasonic - Sony's arch-rival   and the key factor in VHS winning over Betamax. Their allies included a gang of 10 companies  - mostly home electronics manufacturers   and the movie studios with Warner leading the way. ## Vaporware versus Patents So on one side, we had  MMCD. On the other side, SD. The SD Gang argued that SD  was the technically superior   approach that met all the studios'  requirements - including playtime.   In September 1994, a Warners  executive told the Los Angeles Times: > Ours has a higher data capacity. The higher  data capacity, the longer the running time,   the higher the data transfer rate, the higher  the picture quality, the more audio channels,   and the more capacity for multiple  soundtracks and multiple subtitle tracks. The MMCD crowd argued that their technology  built off the successful audio CD ecosystem.   An MMCD player can play existing CDs.   This minimized customer confusion  and ensured backwards compatibility. Moreover, they attacked the SD product as  theoretical and un-manufacturable at volume.   The bonding of the two half-discs had to  be done perfectly without voids or bubbles.   So in essence, they were calling it vaporware. But the SD folks had their own issues with MMCD.  More than a few people grumbled about the rich   patent fees that Philips and its partners  were making from the audio CD bonanza. The exact amount that Sony and Philips have  made from audio CD royalties is not public,   but contemporary estimates pegged  it at about 3 cents for each CD.   In 1993, 1.4 billion CDs were manufactured,  yielding a nice $42 million in royalties. To the SD folks, this was a butt-naked attempt  to bring the CD gravy train to digital video.   They reached out to the US Justice Department  - which was then already investigating Philips   and Sony for anti-competitive patenting  practices - and presented their case. ## The Path to War The CD-ROM's increasing success as  a data storage format meant that   the computer-makers had a stake in the game too. In late April 1995, five big computer  companies - Apple, Compaq, HP, IBM,   and Microsoft - came together to  urge the two sides to set aside   their quarrels and make peace. But  both sides refused to compromise. Norio Ohga, Sony's chairman and CEO,  vigorously argued for their disc.   He told the press in May 1995 that "a split  on the standard is unavoidable because we are   in a world of democracy". To him, this was  a question of "liberalism and democracy". Then in a surprising twist, the MMCD  camp announced that they would adopt   their own dual-layer technology licensed from 3M.   3M's technology stamped a second layer of  pits onto a transparent layer on a disc. This approach differed from  Toshiba's wafer bonding approach,   but it narrowed the gap between the  two disc formats' data capacities. Frankly, nobody wanted another VHS-Betamax  - which was horrific for everyone involved   and confused the customer to no end.  There was so much money at stake. But both sides refused to back down. The  LA Times in July 1995 had a wonderful set   of quotes from everyone on each side.  Philips' lead man Jan Oosterveld said: > "If they say they want one format, then  I would like to hear what they propose.   We have invited people to join us since last year" Lieberfarb retorted: > "We've issued three invitations  for them to talk and ... no response.   This is about Sony and Philips trying to maintain  their hegemony over optical disc technology" Sony's then-President Nobuyuki  Idei told the press in June 1995: > "Do you want to turn over your CD? We  have no intention to compromise on that.   That would not be to the benefit of the consumer" He means literally, physically turning  over the disc inside the player.   Toshiba's senior manager Koji Hase snapped back: > "He always says that about turning over the  disc. It's so craftily done. But it's not true.   Ours has more room on one side than theirs.  How can we support a lesser format?" As the summer of 1995 came to a close, it became  increasingly clear that the two sides were heading   to war, err to market. MMCD said they were  going to launch before the winter holiday.   SD was insistent on launching  mid-1996. Here we go again. ## IBM In the end, it took the computer makers - led by  a third-party kingmaker - to break the deadlock. In August 1995, the technical group of  seven computer-makers issued a press   release saying that both formats met all the  requirements for next generation data storage. The only thing missing was a single,  unified format. The computer-makers   said in their press release that it will not  back either format until they consolidated.   They were obviously trying to  force the two sides together. When that failed, IBM - led by noted optical  disc expert Alan Bell, who brought in IBM   chairman and CEO Lou Gerstner himself - went  to Sony and Philips and told them if they did   not come to a compromise within a few weeks,  then IBM intended to publicly come out for SD. This finally got things rolling. On August  24th, the two sides announced that they   were meeting to hammer out a combined  standard with aspects of both sides. The resulting format had SD's bonded  substrates and error correction plus   MMCD's data modulation scheme,  which encodes digital 1s and 0s   to the sequence of pits and lands to  read. Kind of like a spelling system. Adopting the MMCD scheme slightly reduced disc  capacity from 5 gigabytes to the now-famous   number of 4.7 gigabytes. SD grumbled but IBM  said they didn't care about 0.3 gigabytes. What should they call it? The  journalist Stewart Wolpin in   a very excellent piece from 2007 - go  read it - reported a tussle on naming.   Sony and Philips wanted "CD" in  the name so IBM suggested SMCD. The SD people were a hard NO on that.  So they picked up a colloquial nickname   that had been floating around for the  past year, Digital Video Disc, DVD. Except DVD was supposed to do data storage  too, so they changed the V to Versatile.   Officially DVD just means DVD. In December 1995,  the two sides put together the DVD Consortium,   which handled and guided the  standard. Today that's the DVD forum. ## Closing the Movie Studios The final thing was getting the movie studios  to actually release their movies on DVD. But then arose a new major  sticking point: Copy protection.   The studios worried that releasing  DVDs would enable people to rip   perfect digital copies of their movies.  Particularly with DVD-ROM systems. Toshiba, Matsushita and others hammered  out an acceptable copy protection scheme,   which took a substantial amount  of time. Unsure about piracy,   studios like Paramount, Dreamworks and Fox  initially held their movies from the DVD roster. Toshiba announced that the first DVD players will  enter the market in late 1996, launching in Japan   first. In September, Toshiba announced the SD-3000  DVD player, which began selling in November 1996.   The next month, Warner Brothers released  four of their movies on DVD in Japan. The US launch followed a few  months later in March 1997,   with at least 20 companies launching  players priced between $600 and $1,000   and about ~30 titles priced in $20. By  June that would grow to about 120 titles. ## Conclusion Between the studio holdouts, the high  initial price of DVD player hardware,   and other drama llamas like the "DivX affair", it  took some time for the DVD boom to get started. Sales were laggy throughout 1997 and 1998.   The movie studios were still in wait-and-see mode  - though they were slowly expanding their reach.   Some like Paramount would not release  DVDs of their movies until late 1998. On the computer side, DVD-ROM drives failed  to make much headway in part because of high   costs and Sony and Philips releasing the  rewritable and popular CD-RW standard. By the end of December 1997, there were  just 340,000 DVD players sold in the US   compared to the expected 1.2  million. So initial disappointment. But as the bugs got worked out, and more  titles were released, things picked up.   In April 1998, a new online service  called Netflix launched a DVD rental   by mail business, which quickly gained traction. The 1998 holiday season sold well, and then 1999  saw volumes take off with the release of cheap   $200 DVD players from China. Momentum continued  in 2000 with Sony's Playstation 2, a video game   console that put DVD into millions of people's  homes. Ten million were sold by March 2001. In 2001, US consumer DVD and VHS purchases  reached parity - $5 billion each.   The DVD boom - however short it would  ultimately last - had gotten under way.

## Sounding the Call
Some time in late August or early September 1994,
representatives from seven of the world's  largest content makers gathered together.
They called for a single worldwide optical disc  standard that they can use for their movies.
There were a few technical requirements. It would  need to have room for a full length feature film,
so about 135 minutes on one side of the disc.
Its picture quality must be superior to that of  an existing high-end video system like LaserDisc.
It had to support surround sound,
multiple languages, and aspect ratios. And it also  had to have copy protection for obvious reasons.
The financial stakes were large.
MGM/United Artists' Home Entertainment  President Richard Cohen told the LA Times:
> "If a digital video disc solution is presented  in a way that large numbers of consumers look at
it and say 'This is better than tape and better  than LaserDisc', then it becomes a mass product
opportunity for people such as us who control  libraries to sell the films all over again"
The record labels made billions from CD.
The studios stood to do just as well or better  from a successful Digital Video Disc format.
The patent-holders of such a standard also stood  to reap millions of dollars from licensing fees.
Various proposals emerged to meet  this request. Amidst the shuffle,
two large camps emerged with  different but similar offerings.
## MMCD
While Warners and Philips  did make some peace in 1993,
Philips eventually left to rejoin Sony  - their successful partner from the CD.
In December 1994, they publicly  announced their next big thing:
Multimedia CD, or MMCD. The original  name was HDCD but that was already taken.
An MMCD was the same size of an audio CD with  each side able to store far more data - about
3.7 gigabytes. That lets you put about 135  minutes of video onto a single disc side
which met the requirements just barely.
The MMCD alliance had signed 14 initial  backers, mostly hardware companies like Nokia,
Bang and Olufsen, and Ricoh. Sony had bought  the major movie studio Columbia in 1989,
so they too were aligned.
## Super Density
A month after MMCD's announcement, a coven  of Japanese consumer electronics companies
including Toshiba announced their new, different  standard: "Super Disc" or "Super Density Disc".
The Compact Disc surface features a series  of deep pits and flat areas called "lands".
When we read the CD, a laser  scans over the surface.
When the laser light hits a pit, it doesn't  reflect as much as it does when hitting a land.
The subsequent pattern of reflections are  sensed by a photodiode receptor in the machine,
which then produces a digital electric signal  that can be interpreted by a processor.
If we want to put more data onto the disc, we  need to stuff more pits onto the disc surface.
SD did this with smaller pits packed tighter  together - about 0.4 microns large and 0.74
microns apart compared to MMCD's 0.45  microns large and 0.84 microns apart.
This gives the Super Density disc  5 gigabytes of storage on one side
as compared to MMCD's 3.7 gigabytes.
SD has a thinner substrate,  about 0.6 millimeters thick.
This makes it possible to bond  two sides together back to back,
creating 8-9 gigabytes of total storage across  both sides. But you will need to flip the disc.
Super Disc also offered an optional  second approach for even more capacity:
Dual layers. The first information  layer, let's call it Layer A,
is semi-transparent. The second information  layer, Layer B, is fully reflective.
Layer A being semi-transparent means  that it can reflect just enough light
for its pits to be read by the  laser if focused directly on it.
But at the same time, the laser can  also fire through it to focus on and
read from Layer B below. I know,  right? Doesn't that sound crazy?
This makes it possible to get up  to 10 gigabytes on a single side.
The SD Alliance composed of seven companies,  mostly Japanese consumer electronics companies,
led by Toshiba and Matsushita  or Panasonic - Sony's arch-rival
and the key factor in VHS winning over Betamax.
Their allies included a gang of 10 companies  - mostly home electronics manufacturers
and the movie studios with Warner leading the way.
## Vaporware versus Patents
So on one side, we had  MMCD. On the other side, SD.
The SD Gang argued that SD  was the technically superior
approach that met all the studios'  requirements - including playtime.
In September 1994, a Warners  executive told the Los Angeles Times:
> Ours has a higher data capacity. The higher  data capacity, the longer the running time,
the higher the data transfer rate, the higher  the picture quality, the more audio channels,
and the more capacity for multiple  soundtracks and multiple subtitle tracks.
The MMCD crowd argued that their technology  built off the successful audio CD ecosystem.
An MMCD player can play existing CDs.
This minimized customer confusion  and ensured backwards compatibility.
Moreover, they attacked the SD product as  theoretical and un-manufacturable at volume.
The bonding of the two half-discs had to  be done perfectly without voids or bubbles.
So in essence, they were calling it vaporware.
But the SD folks had their own issues with MMCD.  More than a few people grumbled about the rich
patent fees that Philips and its partners  were making from the audio CD bonanza.
The exact amount that Sony and Philips have  made from audio CD royalties is not public,
but contemporary estimates pegged  it at about 3 cents for each CD.
In 1993, 1.4 billion CDs were manufactured,  yielding a nice $42 million in royalties.
To the SD folks, this was a butt-naked attempt  to bring the CD gravy train to digital video.
They reached out to the US Justice Department  - which was then already investigating Philips
and Sony for anti-competitive patenting  practices - and presented their case.
## The Path to War
The CD-ROM's increasing success as  a data storage format meant that
the computer-makers had a stake in the game too.
In late April 1995, five big computer  companies - Apple, Compaq, HP, IBM,
and Microsoft - came together to  urge the two sides to set aside
their quarrels and make peace. But  both sides refused to compromise.
Norio Ohga, Sony's chairman and CEO,  vigorously argued for their disc.
He told the press in May 1995 that "a split  on the standard is unavoidable because we are
in a world of democracy". To him, this was  a question of "liberalism and democracy".
Then in a surprising twist, the MMCD  camp announced that they would adopt
their own dual-layer technology licensed from 3M.
3M's technology stamped a second layer of  pits onto a transparent layer on a disc.
This approach differed from  Toshiba's wafer bonding approach,
but it narrowed the gap between the  two disc formats' data capacities.
Frankly, nobody wanted another VHS-Betamax  - which was horrific for everyone involved
and confused the customer to no end.  There was so much money at stake.
But both sides refused to back down. The  LA Times in July 1995 had a wonderful set
of quotes from everyone on each side.  Philips' lead man Jan Oosterveld said:
> "If they say they want one format, then  I would like to hear what they propose.
We have invited people to join us since last year"
Lieberfarb retorted:
> "We've issued three invitations  for them to talk and ... no response.
This is about Sony and Philips trying to maintain  their hegemony over optical disc technology"
Sony's then-President Nobuyuki  Idei told the press in June 1995:
> "Do you want to turn over your CD? We  have no intention to compromise on that.
That would not be to the benefit of the consumer"
He means literally, physically turning  over the disc inside the player.
Toshiba's senior manager Koji Hase snapped back:
> "He always says that about turning over the  disc. It's so craftily done. But it's not true.
Ours has more room on one side than theirs.  How can we support a lesser format?"
As the summer of 1995 came to a close, it became  increasingly clear that the two sides were heading
to war, err to market. MMCD said they were  going to launch before the winter holiday.
SD was insistent on launching  mid-1996. Here we go again.
## IBM
In the end, it took the computer makers - led by  a third-party kingmaker - to break the deadlock.
In August 1995, the technical group of  seven computer-makers issued a press
release saying that both formats met all the  requirements for next generation data storage.
The only thing missing was a single,  unified format. The computer-makers
said in their press release that it will not  back either format until they consolidated.
They were obviously trying to  force the two sides together.
When that failed, IBM - led by noted optical  disc expert Alan Bell, who brought in IBM
chairman and CEO Lou Gerstner himself - went  to Sony and Philips and told them if they did
not come to a compromise within a few weeks,  then IBM intended to publicly come out for SD.
This finally got things rolling. On August  24th, the two sides announced that they
were meeting to hammer out a combined  standard with aspects of both sides.
The resulting format had SD's bonded  substrates and error correction plus
MMCD's data modulation scheme,  which encodes digital 1s and 0s
to the sequence of pits and lands to  read. Kind of like a spelling system.
Adopting the MMCD scheme slightly reduced disc  capacity from 5 gigabytes to the now-famous
number of 4.7 gigabytes. SD grumbled but IBM  said they didn't care about 0.3 gigabytes.
What should they call it? The  journalist Stewart Wolpin in
a very excellent piece from 2007 - go  read it - reported a tussle on naming.
Sony and Philips wanted "CD" in  the name so IBM suggested SMCD.
The SD people were a hard NO on that.  So they picked up a colloquial nickname
that had been floating around for the  past year, Digital Video Disc, DVD.
Except DVD was supposed to do data storage  too, so they changed the V to Versatile.
Officially DVD just means DVD. In December 1995,  the two sides put together the DVD Consortium,
which handled and guided the  standard. Today that's the DVD forum.
## Closing the Movie Studios
The final thing was getting the movie studios  to actually release their movies on DVD.
But then arose a new major  sticking point: Copy protection.
The studios worried that releasing  DVDs would enable people to rip
perfect digital copies of their movies.  Particularly with DVD-ROM systems.
Toshiba, Matsushita and others hammered  out an acceptable copy protection scheme,
which took a substantial amount  of time. Unsure about piracy,
studios like Paramount, Dreamworks and Fox  initially held their movies from the DVD roster.
Toshiba announced that the first DVD players will  enter the market in late 1996, launching in Japan
first. In September, Toshiba announced the SD-3000  DVD player, which began selling in November 1996.
The next month, Warner Brothers released  four of their movies on DVD in Japan.
The US launch followed a few  months later in March 1997,
with at least 20 companies launching  players priced between $600 and $1,000
and about ~30 titles priced in $20. By  June that would grow to about 120 titles.
## Conclusion
Between the studio holdouts, the high  initial price of DVD player hardware,
and other drama llamas like the "DivX affair", it  took some time for the DVD boom to get started.
Sales were laggy throughout 1997 and 1998.
The movie studios were still in wait-and-see mode  - though they were slowly expanding their reach.
Some like Paramount would not release  DVDs of their movies until late 1998.
On the computer side, DVD-ROM drives failed  to make much headway in part because of high
costs and Sony and Philips releasing the  rewritable and popular CD-RW standard.
By the end of December 1997, there were  just 340,000 DVD players sold in the US
compared to the expected 1.2  million. So initial disappointment.
But as the bugs got worked out, and more  titles were released, things picked up.
In April 1998, a new online service  called Netflix launched a DVD rental
by mail business, which quickly gained traction.
The 1998 holiday season sold well, and then 1999  saw volumes take off with the release of cheap
$200 DVD players from China. Momentum continued  in 2000 with Sony's Playstation 2, a video game
console that put DVD into millions of people's  homes. Ten million were sold by March 2001.
In 2001, US consumer DVD and VHS purchases  reached parity - $5 billion each.
The DVD boom - however short it would  ultimately last - had gotten under way.
